strengths: Introduces a well-motivated physics-informed input descriptor (the zeroth-step Hamiltonian H(0)) that replaces arbitrary learned atom/edge embeddings, is cheap to compute, and empirically enables good out-of-distribution behavior for an unseen element (Ne) and dramatically shrinks the residual regression target.

Extends the TraceGrad mechanism from a simple GNN backbone to a Transformer architecture with persistent, updated edge features, providing a principled way to combine strict E(3)/O(3) equivariance with non-linear expressiveness for an edge-level (rather than node-level) prediction task.

Provides a rigorous theoretical treatment of the gauge freedom in Hamiltonian regression and of error amplification from the ill-conditioned overlap matrix in reciprocal space, and translates this analysis into a concrete joint R-space/k-space loss with an explicit P-Q decoupling penalty that is shown (via ablations and qualitative band-structure plots) to suppress 'ghost states'.

Curates and releases a large, chemically diverse benchmark dataset (Materials-HAM-SOC: 17,000 structures, 60+ elements, up to f-orbitals, explicit SOC) which fills a real gap in open Hamiltonian-prediction datasets and could be a useful community resource.

Thorough ablation study (Table 4, Appendix L) isolating the contribution of each proposed component (input descriptor, delta-learning target, TraceGrad, ensemble, k-space loss, PQ penalty) with consistent, interpretable trends and qualitative band-structure visualizations across many representative test structures.

Reports a fairly complete efficiency analysis (Table 3) showing large practical speedups over DFT with a sensible breakdown of computational stages, and includes gauge-invariant, element-wise, and downstream-observable (band structure, conductivity) evaluations rather than relying on a single aggregate error metric.
weaknesses: The comparison to prior universal/general Hamiltonian-prediction work is narrow: only DeepH-E3 and the original TraceGrad backbone are directly benchmarked, while other relevant recent universal or broad-coverage models mentioned in related work (e.g., DeepH-2, QHNet, Zhong et al. 2024's universal ML Kohn-Sham Hamiltonian) are discussed qualitatively but never compared quantitatively, making the 'state-of-the-art' and 'universal' claims harder to fully substantiate.

The reported gap versus DeepH-E3 on Materials-HAM-SOC is very large (12.6 meV vs 1.417 meV, ~9x), which is somewhat suspicious given DeepH-E3 is a reasonably mature equivariant method; it is unclear whether DeepH-E3 was tuned/trained to convergence under comparable compute/hyperparameter budgets, raising a fairness concern about baseline strength.

The out-of-distribution generalization claim is supported by a single case study (one Ne-containing structure), which is too limited to substantiate a general claim about extrapolation to unseen elements; the authors themselves acknowledge this is left to future work.

The ensemble-of-4-sub-models design adds noticeable complexity/inference cost (per Appendix I, 4 GPUs are used just for one sample's inference), but the paper does not analyze the accuracy-vs-cost trade-off of the ensemble relative to a single larger model, nor report parameter counts/FLOPs for the full framework versus baselines.

The dataset appears restricted to nonmagnetic compounds and the training pipeline uses a single fixed random seed with no reported variance across runs/splits, limiting confidence in the statistical robustness of the reported gains, especially for the more marginal ablations (e.g., Ablation@Loss-PQ vs Full Method, 1.496 vs 1.417 meV).

Some claims (e.g., 'establish NextHAM as a universal and highly accurate deep learning model') are stated quite strongly in the abstract/conclusion relative to the evidence, which is largely confined to one curated dataset plus two small specialized datasets (MG/MM), rather than external, independently curated benchmarks.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: building a more generalizable deep-learning Hamiltonian predictor across a broad span of the periodic table with explicit SOC, rather than restricting to single material systems as much prior work does.

The zeroth-step Hamiltonian H^(0), derived from the DFT initial charge density, is a physically well-motivated input feature and correction target; it is cheap to compute (no diagonalization) and empirically closes a large fraction of the gap to the self-consistent Hamiltonian, simplifying the learning problem.

Extension of the TraceGrad SO(3)-invariant/equivariant nonlinearity mechanism to a Transformer-style (Equiformer-inspired) architecture with explicit, persistently maintained edge features is a reasonable and non-trivial architectural contribution for an edge-level (Hamiltonian) regression task.

The joint real-space/k-space training objective with an explicit P/Q subspace decomposition and PQ-coupling penalty is a thoughtful, theoretically grounded (condition-number/ghost-state analysis in Appendix A.2) way to address a known pathology (ghost states from ill-conditioned overlap matrices) that purely real-space losses miss.
A new, reasonably large and chemically diverse dataset (17,000 structures, 68 elements, SOC, high-quality NAO basis) is contributed and could be a useful community resource if released.

Thorough ablation study (Table 4, Figs. 8-9) isolates the contribution of each proposed component (input descriptor, output target, TraceGrad, ensemble, k-loss, PQ loss) and provides visual evidence that the PQ penalty specifically suppresses ghost states in band structures.
Runtime analysis (Table 3) convincingly demonstrates large speedups over DFT self-consistent cycles, with reasonable discussion of scaling behavior (O(N) vs O(TN^3)).
weaknesses: No comparison against any existing Hamiltonian-prediction baseline (e.g., DeepH, QHNet, DeepH-2, TraceGrad/its original GNN backbone, DeepH-E3) on the new Materials-HAM-SOC benchmark or on any shared benchmark. All quantitative results are internal ablations against the authors' own full method; without an external baseline it is impossible to assess whether the claimed accuracy/generalization gains are actually superior to prior state of the art, which is a major gap for a paper whose central claim is improved universality/generalization over existing methods.

The headline sub-μeV accuracy for the spin-off-diagonal (↑↓, ↓↑) blocks and near-perfect match of H^(0) to H^(T) in these blocks appears largely attributable to time-reversal symmetry making these blocks trivially small/near-zero in the tested (apparently mostly non-magnetic) systems, rather than a genuine demonstration of the model's SOC-handling capability; this should be discussed more critically rather than emphasized as a headline result.

The dataset construction samples 17,000 'nonmagnetic' compounds from the Materials Project; restricting to nonmagnetic systems while claiming to 'explicitly incorporate SOC effects' and target broad generalization is a notable scope limitation that is not adequately flagged in the abstract/intro, and may inflate apparent accuracy on spin-related blocks.

No error bars, multiple-seed runs, or statistical significance testing are reported; a single fixed random seed is used throughout (Appendix A.5), which weakens confidence in the reported single-point accuracy numbers, especially for ablation comparisons where the reported differences (e.g., 1.417 vs 1.496 meV) are numerically small.

It is unclear whether the Materials-HAM-SOC dataset and code will be publicly released; without this, reproducibility of both the benchmark and the method is uncertain, which is especially important given the dataset is a central claimed contribution.

The paper does not report per-property downstream accuracy metrics beyond qualitative band-structure visual comparisons (Figs. 8-9); quantitative downstream metrics (e.g., band gap MAE, DOS error, or eigenvalue MAE near the Fermi level) across the full test set would substantiate the qualitative 'excellent agreement' claims more rigorously.

The ensemble strategy (4 sub-models over distance ranges) and 4-GPU/one-model-per-GPU training/inference setup raises questions about fairness of the runtime comparison against DFT (single-node CPU) and about the practical resource cost of NextHAM relative to a single monolithic model; the paper does not report the accuracy/cost trade-off of using fewer sub-models.

Related work discussion, while reasonably thorough, does not clearly quantify how NextHAM's scope (68 elements, up to f orbitals, SOC) numerically compares to concurrent broad-coverage efforts such as Zhong et al. (2025)'s universal SOC Hamiltonian model, beyond a brief qualitative mention; a more direct comparison (even from reported numbers in that paper) would strengthen the positioning claim of being 'universal.'
